to install fixed version of MSstatsLOBD.

Kind regards,
Mateusz

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

if you want to keep these rows, you will need to use the extended workflow from MSstatsConvert package and replace our MSstatsClean method for Skyline files with your own code that doesn't filter by Truncated column. You can do that by adjusting the code from converters.R file from MSstats package and .cleanSkyline function from MSstatsConvert package. Currently, keeping Truncated rows is not a option in ou converter.

Kind regards,
Mateusz

messages.subject: Re: feature subset in dataprocess
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julie,

You can think of it as a fancy median. When there are no outliers and no missing values, the protein-level summaries are very similar to the medians. When there are missing values, the summarization accounts for the missing values (assuming that the majority of missing values are due to the low abundance of the underlying analytes). The summarization also reduces the influence of the outliers.

You can find more info in the videos on the May Institute YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/c/MayInstituteNEU

I hope that this helps at least somewhat. Thank you for using MSstats.
Sincerely
Olga

You must use adjusted p-values if you'd like to make any claims of statistical significance (including error rate control etc).

If you only want to rank protein candidates for a subsequent followup, while ignoring statistical significance, you can use raw p-values. But please keep in mind that this ranking may be unreliable, and can lead to irreproducible results.

Thank you for using MSstats
Sincerely
Olga

> Hi Julie,

> You can think of it as a fancy median. When there are no outliers and no missing values, the protein-level summaries are very similar to the medians. When there are missing values, the summarization accounts for the missing values (assuming that the majority of missing values are due to the low abundance of the underlying analytes). The summarization also reduces the influence of the outliers.
>
> You can find more info in the videos on the May Institute YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/c/MayInstituteNEU

messages.body_plain:
Hi Claus,

There currently is not a specific SILAC pipeline, however we have used MSstatsTMT to analyze SILAC experiments in the past. I am not sure what your exact experimental design is, however you should be able to treat each sample as a "mixture", with the heavy and light cells as "channels". See below for a table of what I mean. With your data in the correct format you can simply follow the standard MSstatsTMT pipeline.

Mixture (Sample)   Channel Condition
1 channel.H       Treatment
1 channel.L    Control
2 channel.H        Treatment
2 channel.L    Control
3 channel.H   Control
3 channel.L       Treatment

We have seen that SILAC experiments can be underpowered, due to a low number of replicates, so if you see few significant proteins after modeling that may be why. Let me know if you have any questions!

Best,
Devon

messages.subject: Re: TMT single mixture analysis: comparison between individual channels?
messages.subject_clean: TMT single mixture analysis: comparison between individual channels?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Salva,

Sorry for not answering sooner. I have several comments:

- Your description of the hypothesis that you'd like to test seems incorrect. I do not know what you mean by 'comparing individual channels'. MSstats compares average protein abundances in the underlying populations of biological subjects. E.g., it would make sense to compare the abundance of a protein treated with a compound X, as summarized across all the biological replicates, vs  the abundance of a protein treated with a compound Y, as summarized across all the biological replicates. Summarizing distinct measurements from multiple biological replicates is important, as it allows us to quantify the extent of biological variation, and distinguish systematic changes due to the treatment from artifacts of random variation.

- If you are indeed interested in comparing treated vs untreated subjects, then your experimental design is suboptimal. The mix of 3 biological samples does not give us an opportunity to quantify the between-subject variation. It has a different biological variation than an individual biological sample, but there is no way to communicate it to MSstats. It is still possible to make these comparisons in R (while making stronger statistical assumptions), however it is not possible to do this with a default implementation in MSstats.

- If you are interested in comparing the compounds with MSstats, I suggest that you drop the channel that contains a mix of untreated subjects from the analysis. You will be able to compare the compounds from the resulting dataset. (Frequently such mixes are used as a reference channel, to improve selection of peptides for fragmentation, or as normalization when your experiment has multiple mixtures. But since you only have one mixture, at the stage of statistical analysis it does more harm than good.)

I hope that this helps at least somewhat
Olga

OV
